name: Umar Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Umar Chen, 43, and I run equipment at a large mine. I do the morning inspection, climb into the loader, move rock where dispatch sends me and try to notice when the ground or machine doesn't match the sheet. I'm still a junior operator and learn a lot from the older hands; I like getting a difficult load right, but the long shifts and my lower pay wear on me. At home my partner Leila and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and less than a month's expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AI Plateau sounds like the software we already have: useful for a form, useless for moving rock. We still have to watch the loader's blind side and listen when a belt sounds wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a steady mine would be a relief, but steady wages still leave us with less than a month's bills saved. My partner Leila works part time at a bakery, and when her shifts dip the mortgage feels very large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my equipment shifts and use the phone AI to explain the maintenance terms I don't yet know. In the first year I'd put the small overtime payments against the credit card, provided overtime is offered; I can't promise money we haven't earned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel relieved about my job and still tight in the chest when the mortgage payment comes round. A quiet technology story doesn't make our kitchen table arithmetic quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the shift are you still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I used my phone to ask what a hydraulic warning meant, then checked it with the senior operator before touching anything. I was embarrassed to ask him twice, but a wrong guess on a loader is worse than looking new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What already gets cut at home when money is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I already stopped buying takeaway on Fridays after her bakery lost two evening shifts. I'd rather keep that small family treat, but I can't call us secure while the card balance is there.

say: I would tell the crew that **forms get quicker**, but we still have to watch the equipment.
I would say the mine seems **steady**, although I would not claim every worker is secure.
think: I would welcome a **steady wage**, because our savings cover less than one month.
My partner’s **bakery shifts** can fall, which makes the mortgage harder to carry.
do: Keep taking **loader shifts** and check unfamiliar warning terms with the senior operator.
Put offered **overtime pay** toward the credit card during the first year.
feel: Relieved about the work, but **tense** when the mortgage comes due.
S0.quote: A quiet technology story doesn't make our kitchen table arithmetic quiet.
fieldNote: Umar separates stable mine work from the household’s **thin cushion** and variable bakery pay.
He uses AI daily for **learning**, yet checks equipment decisions with a senior operator.

steps.text: Keep taking equipment shifts at the mine
Use phone AI to explain unfamiliar maintenance terms
Put any offered overtime pay against the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption should come with paid training, not a memo telling people to manage alone. The planning office may get smaller before anyone puts a robot beside my loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I know my work is mostly hands and eyes, but I am the newest operator on my shift. If fewer office people plan the loads, management might ask the rest of us to do more, and I don't know whether the lower-paid hands go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union steward about a paid equipment certificate and put my name down if the mine funds it. In the first year I'd learn the new dispatch screen with the experienced operator and keep applying for shifts; I won't leave a wage before another one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about the screen and nervous about being measured by it. My income could shrink through lost shifts even if no one calls it a layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who comes to mind when you say the office might shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch clerk, Nia, helped me read my first load sheet, and I worry about her job first. Our shifts depend on her corrections when the printed route doesn't match the ground, so losing that judgment could hurt us too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that training possible for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the training on paid time because evenings are when I collect our two children from school care. I can learn a new system, but I can't pay for a course and childcare together with our savings.

say: I would ask for **paid training** as planning and checking move into software.
I would tell coworkers that **dispatch judgment** still matters when the route and ground disagree.
think: I am the **newest operator**, so lost shifts could hit me before established workers.
I worry that a smaller **planning office** will push more work onto the equipment crew.
do: Ask the **union steward** about a mine-funded equipment certificate and enroll if funded.
Learn the new **dispatch screen** with a senior operator while continuing paid shifts.
feel: Curious about the tools, but **nervous** about losing hours.
S1.quote: I can learn a new system, but I can't pay for a course and childcare together with our savings.
fieldNote: He locates the first pressure in the **planning office**, while fearing lost shifts for junior operators.
His interest in training depends on **paid time** because childcare and savings limit access.

steps.text: Ask the union steward about funded equipment certification
Enroll in equipment certification if the mine pays
Learn the dispatch screen with a senior operator
Keep applying for mine shifts as the system changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2028 is a shock and we need a say before management redraws everyone's work. Thinking AI could take the dispatch and maintenance paperwork by 2028, even though a robot that handles the rock like us isn't due until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three extra years on a machine are not three years of safety. I'd be 45 when the thinking system arrives and 48 when the robots do, with both children still needing things at home and almost no buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start this week by asking the steward for a meeting about paid training and what happens to junior operators. If the mine offers a funded mechanical maintenance course, I'd enroll; during the first year after 2028 I'd keep operating equipment, seek the course, and apply for maintenance openings at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened enough to act, but not frozen. The thought of a machine taking my shift by 2031 makes me look at our mortgage statement in a different way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the three-year gap feel short to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to think the machine was the hard part and the load sheet was only paper. If the software chooses the route and watches the machine, a cheaper robot is a short step from my seat; I don't know whether it can handle every awkward load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family if the hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila the mortgage comes first and the children's swimming lessons may have to pause if my hours fall. I'd hate doing that because the older one has just learned to float, but I won't pretend bakery pay covers our house.

say: I would demand a **worker voice** before the mine changes dispatch and equipment jobs.
I would tell the crew that **robots arrive later**, around 2031, but we need a plan now.
think: I expect thinking AI to take **dispatch paperwork** by 2028 and robots to threaten my seat around 2031.
My **thin savings** and mortgage leave little room to wait for a new job.
do: Request a **steward meeting** this week about junior operators and paid training.
Enroll in **mechanical maintenance** if funded, and apply for mine openings after 2028.
feel: Frightened by a possible **lost shift**, but ready to make calls.
S2.quote: Three extra years on a machine are not three years of safety.
fieldNote: The shorter horizon turns his daily **AI curiosity** into urgent concern about equipment automation.
He names the **mortgage** and children’s swimming lessons as concrete consequences of lost hours.

steps.text: Ask the union steward to convene a junior-operator meeting
Enroll in mechanical maintenance training if the mine funds it
Apply for maintenance openings at the mine after 2028
Keep operating mine equipment during the first year after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people AGI by 2031 gives us time to bargain for a real path into other mine work. Robots around 2034 still put operators at risk, so a promise to watch developments would not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 when thinking AI arrives and 51 when the robots could work the machines. The children would be older, but mortgage payments don't age out, and I cannot assume the mine will keep a junior operator just because I've stayed five more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the training manager what maintenance qualifications the mine actually accepts and compare them with a local college course. If the union wins paid release time, I'd enroll next year; in the first year after 2031 I'd still run equipment while applying for trainee maintenance positions and saving whatever overtime we truly get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than in the 2028 picture because I can build a qualification in stages. I still worry about paying for it and about whether the trainee positions will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a maintenance qualification credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to spot a track that's wearing unevenly now, but I can't repair it yet. A certificate would have to come with workshop hours, or I'd be carrying a piece of paper into a job I couldn't safely do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five years give Leila and me room to clear the credit card if shifts hold. They don't give us a spare income, and I'd be careful not to spend the same overtime twice in our plans.

say: I would push for a **training path** before robots reach equipment work around 2034.
I would reject a vague **wait and see** promise from the mine.
think: I cannot assume **seniority** will protect a junior operator at age 51.
My children will be older, but the **mortgage** will still need paying.
do: Compare accepted **maintenance qualifications** with the local college course now.
Enroll if **paid release time** is won, then apply for trainee openings after 2031.
feel: Less cornered, yet **worried** about course costs and actual vacancies.
S3.quote: A certificate would have to come with workshop hours, or I'd be carrying a piece of paper into a job I couldn't safely do.
fieldNote: He treats the five-year lead as time for **practical training**, not a guarantee of placement.
He checks the qualification against **mine standards** and keeps the family budget tied to actual shifts.

steps.text: Ask the training manager which maintenance qualifications the mine accepts
Enroll in the local course if paid release time is won
Apply for trainee maintenance positions after 2031
Put any actual overtime toward the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to change course, if the mine lets junior people train rather than just the favourites. Robots that can run the equipment around 2039 mean this is still about our jobs, not only office desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robots follow. The children should be grown by then, but I cannot count on retirement at 56 or on a pension I have not earned; I would still need paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the maintenance qualification while I still have a wage, if I can get funded places and real workshop hours. Through 2036 I'd apply for maintenance and safety inspection openings, and in the first year after AGI I'd keep whichever paid mine role I hold while checking whether robots are taking the machine shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more hopeful because I can practice instead of rushing into a course I can't afford. There is still a hard edge to it: ten years is long enough for our children to grow up and for a mine to change its hiring rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family look by the 2036 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger child would be finishing school by 2036, and I'd like to help with their next step rather than ask them to help me. I won't build our plan on them moving out on a particular birthday; children cost money after school too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a maintenance move settle the matter for good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I get into maintenance, I would still watch what robots do to that work around 2039. Repairs can change too, so I would want the union to negotiate paid learning again, not treat one certificate as lifetime cover.

say: I would ask for **fair training places** while the mine has time to prepare.
I would remind coworkers that **equipment robots** still threaten operating jobs around 2039.
think: I will need **paid work** at 56 even if my children are grown.
I cannot count on an **unearned pension** or assume maintenance work stays untouched.
do: Pursue **funded maintenance training** with workshop hours while still earning.
Apply for **maintenance or safety roles** before 2036 and keep paid work after AGI.
feel: Hopeful about practice time, but **uneasy** about future hiring and robot repairs.
S4.quote: I cannot count on retirement at 56 or on a pension I have not earned; I would still need paid work.
fieldNote: The long lead makes him **hopeful** about a real qualification, although he avoids assuming retirement.
He anticipates **grown children** while allowing for continued family costs and a mortgage.

steps.text: Enroll in funded maintenance training with workshop hours if available
Apply for maintenance or safety inspection roles before 2036
Keep paid mine work in the first year after AGI
Ask the union to negotiate further paid learning as robots arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my paperwork changes almost at once and the equipment seat could follow around 2031. I'd need funded training with workshop hours, a fair chance at mine maintenance vacancies, and enough paid time to take the course without missing the mortgage. The union should be in the room when those places are decided.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the first training slot. The people with a small savings account and school pickup don't have the freedom to wait for a course after their shifts disappear. I use AI every day, but knowing how to ask a phone a question is not a new wage.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day, but knowing how to ask a phone a question is not a new wage.
portrait: Umar is a **junior miner** operating equipment at a large mine while learning from experienced workers.
He supports a partner and **two children** with lower pay, variable bakery income and less than one month saved.
He uses **phone AI** readily, but wants funded workshop training before equipment robots threaten his seat.
The **2028 scenario** scares him most because its short lead meets a mortgage and thin savings.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because robot equipment work could follow around 2031 before he has retrained.
whatWouldHelp: He asks for **funded workshop training**, paid time and fair access to mine maintenance openings.
He wants the **union present** when training places are allocated.
